“I am not a weed,” the flower had replied gently.

“Forgive me...”

“I am not afraid of tigers, but I have a horror of drafts. Wouldn't you happen to have a screen?”

“‘A horror of drafts’...that is unfortunate for a plant,” the little prince had remarked. “This flower is certainly complicated...”

“In the evening you will put me under a glass globe. It is very cold where you live. It is poorly set up here. Where I come from...”

But she had broken off. She had come in the form of a seed. She could not have known anything of other worlds. Humiliated at having let herself be caught preparing so naïve a lie, she had coughed two or three times, to put the little prince in the wrong:

“That screen?...”

“I was just going to get it, but you were talking to me!”

Then she had forced her cough so as to make him feel guilty all the same.

Thus the little prince, despite the goodwill of his love, had quickly begun to doubt her. He had taken unimportant words seriously and had become very unhappy.

“I should not have listened to her,” he confided to me one day. “One must never listen to flowers. One must look at them and breathe in their fragrance. Mine filled my planet with fragrance, but I did not know how to take pleasure in it. That business about the claws, which had annoyed me so much, should have moved me...”

He confided further:

“I did not understand anything then! I should have judged her by her actions and not by her words. She filled my world with fragrance and light. I should never have run away! I should have guessed her tenderness behind her poor little tricks. Flowers are so contradictory! But I was too young to know how to love her.”

CHAPTER IX

I believe that, for his escape, he took advantage of a migration of wild birds. On the morning of his departure, he put his planet carefully in order. He thoroughly swept out his active volcanoes. He had two active volcanoes. And they were very convenient for heating breakfast in the morning. He also had an extinct volcano. But, as he said, “You never know!” So he swept out the extinct volcano as well. If they are well swept out, volcanoes burn gently and regularly, without eruptions. Volcanic eruptions are like chimney fires. Obviously, here on our Earth we are much too small to sweep out our volcanoes. That is why they cause us all sorts of trouble.

The little prince also pulled up, with a little melancholy, the last baobab shoots. He believed that he was never to return. But all these familiar tasks seemed extremely sweet to him that morning. And when he watered the flower one last time and prepared to shelter her under her glass globe, he found himself wanting to cry.

“Goodbye,” he said to the flower.

But she did not answer him.

“Goodbye,” he repeated.

The flower coughed. But it was not because of her cold.

“I have been foolish,” she finally said to him. “I ask your forgiveness. Try to be happy.”

He was surprised by the absence of reproaches. He remained there, completely bewildered, holding the glass globe in the air. He did not understand this calm gentleness.

“But of course I love you,” the flower said to him. “You knew nothing of it, through my fault. That is of no importance. But you have been as foolish as I have. Try to be happy...Leave that glass globe alone. I do not want it anymore.”

“But the wind...”

“My cold is not as bad as all that...The cool night air will do me good. I am a flower.”

“But the animals...”

“I must put up with two or three caterpillars if I want to know the butterflies. They say they are so beautiful. Otherwise, who will visit me? You will be far away. As for large animals, I am not afraid of anything. I have my claws.”

And she naïvely displayed her four thorns. Then she added:

“Do not linger like this; it is irritating. You have decided to leave. Go away.”

For she did not want him to see her cry. She was such a proud flower...

CHAPTER X

He was in the region of asteroids 325, 326, 327, 328, 329, and 330. So he began by visiting them, to look for something to do there and to educate himself.

The first was inhabited by a king. The king sat, dressed in purple and ermine, upon a very simple yet majestic throne.

“Ah! Here is a subject!” cried the king when he caught sight of the little prince.

And the little prince wondered:

“How can he recognize me when he has never seen me before?”

He did not know that, for kings, the world is greatly simplified. All men are subjects.

“Come closer so that I may see you better,” said the king, who was very proud to be king over someone at last.

The little prince looked around for somewhere to sit, but the planet was entirely encumbered by the magnificent ermine robe. So he remained standing, and, as he was tired, he yawned.

“It is contrary to etiquette to yawn in the presence of a king,” the monarch told him. “I forbid you to do so.”

“I cannot help it,” replied the little prince, utterly embarrassed. “I have made a long journey, and I have not slept...”

“Then,” said the king, “I order you to yawn. I have not seen anyone yawn for years. Yawns are curiosities to me. Come now! Yawn again. That is an order.”

“It makes me self-conscious...I cannot do it anymore...” said the little prince, blushing deeply.

“Hum! Hum!” replied the king. “Then I...I order you sometimes to yawn and sometimes to...”

He stammered a little and seemed offended.

For the king considered it essential that his authority be respected. He tolerated no disobedience. He was an absolute monarch. But, since he was very good, he gave reasonable orders.

“If I ordered,” he would commonly say, “if I ordered a general to turn himself into a seabird, and if the general did not obey, it would not be the general's fault. It would be my fault.”

“May I sit down?” the little prince asked timidly.

“I order you to sit down,” the king replied, majestically gathering up one side of his ermine robe.

But the little prince was puzzled. The planet was tiny. What could the king possibly rule over?

“Sire,” he said to him...“I beg your pardon for questioning you...”
